existing single line is already the correct hook and needs no change:

      const tether = a.t < a.tether ? 0.5 : 1;   // Tether: hold the rail
      const pull = K.bowl * g.bowl * tether * rad * (1 - K.ridgeFall * over * over);

Read site: stepTop section 4, BOWL + RIDGE, before the radial velocity update.
It must multiply `pull` and not `K.bowl`, so the rig multiplier g.bowl and the

notes:
FINDING 1, THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Bite as specified in HANDOFF section 7 does nothing. Tripling `gear` raises the friction coefficient mu, but jt is clamped to `K.muMax * |jn| * K.jtCap`, and on real builds it is already saturated against that clamp by an order of magnitude. Measured on the attack against balance reference pair: rim speed 21.2 m/s, inv 53.1, sqrt(gearA*gearB) about 0.92, so raw jt is about 0.368 while jn is about 0.017 and the cap is about 0.032. Saturated 11.7 times over. Tripling gear moves the outcome by zero, exactly as the RIG_NEUTRAL comment records happening to Spin Thief. Bite therefore has to lift jtCap, and my collide hook does. Do not merge the gear multiplier without the cap lift.

FINDING 2. The echo body currently in the file saves a copy of a.spec before the inner fire and restores from that copy afterwards. Reversal, Shed and Scatter all REPLACE a.spec, so those mutations are silently discarded; an echoed Reversal ends up with a.w flipped and spec.dir unflipped, which makes drive push against the rotation for the rest of the round. My version restores from the current a.spec and only overwrites the `ability` field. This is a correctness fix, not a taste call.

FINDING 3. `cornered` and `onRidge` were reading different lines. ridgeT accumulated only above `over > 0.35`, which is radius above 0.818 of the arena, while onRidge fires at 0.72. A top can sit in the band between them indefinitely, satisfying onRidge and never becoming cornered. My hook splits the two: charge keeps the tuned 0.35 band, ridgeT starts at ridgeAt.

BITE PAYS ONLY WHILE YOU ARE SLOWER, and this is intended. Working the tangential solver through: for opposite spins jt transfers from the faster rim to the slower one, so a biting top that is ahead on spin gives some away. That makes Bite a natural partner for the `behind` and `lowSpin` triggers and a trap on `charged`. For mirror spins both tops bleed and the one with more rim inertia loses less, which gives a heavy wide blade a real reason to carry it. The description says so honestly rather than promising a steal.

PITCH DEVIATES FROM THE ONE LINE SPEC, deliberately. A shove applied at any range reads as telekinesis and fails the no caption rule, so I gated it on a linear falloff from rim contact to a three centimetre gap and scaled the spin cost by the same factor. A whiffed pitch still costs the round's only ability. If you would rather have the unconditional version, delete the `reach` term and the `if`, but then check what it looks like on screen before shipping it.

BACKSPIN AND THE `opposite` TEST. collide computes `opposite` from Math.sign(a.w) and Math.sign(b.w), not from the backspin flipped signs, so the Spin Thief rig's stealOpp multiplier ignores backspin. I left it alone on purpose: `opposite` is also returned in the collide payload and the UI reports actual spin directions to the player. If you decide the rig should see the effective sign, the one line is `const opposite = Math.sign(sgnA * a.w) !== Math.sign(sgnB * b.w);`, but that changes the returned payload too, so do it in its own commit with harness numbers either side.

TRIGGER LABELS ARE HALF THE TRUTH. triggerReady returns false above the switch whenever `a.charge < 1`, so `late` really means eight seconds AND charged, and `mirror` means same spin AND charged. That is right, because charge is the universal economy and nothing should bypass it, but the workshop's two line program will read as a lie on a build that never charges. Consider prefixing the program display with the charge condition once, above both lines, rather than editing TRIGGER_LABEL.

STONESKIN IS NOT A BETTER ANCHOR. It cuts the shock drain through `taken` but not the tilt, because the lean bump reads `absorb`. Anchor does the opposite: it forces lean back down and multiplies exitNeed by six but does nothing about spin loss. They are answers to different deaths, spinout and knockout, and neither dominates.

WHAT TO RUN AFTER WIRING. `node test/determinism.js` first, because echo recurses and a recursion is exactly the kind of thing that reads a random number one extra time; the seeded stream law means new code must consume zero dice headless. Then `node tools/harness2.js 300` for ALL ACCEPTANCE TARGETS MET, then `node tools/partaudit.js 800 2` once the eight new cores that carry these abilities exist, since the plus four mean point gate lands on the cores and not on the abilities in isolation. Bite's 2.2 cap lift and pitch's 1.90 shove are the two numbers most likely to need retuning; change those before touching anything in K.

VISIBILITY AUDIT, honestly. Six of the eight are unmistakable without a caption: tether, scatter, stoneskin, pitch, wind up and backspin all change the shape of the motion within a frame or two. Echo is visible only as a repeat of a motion the viewer saw moments ago, which needs the two tops to be doing different things for it to read at all. Bite is the weakest of the eight, because a spin transfer is a bar moving and not a body moving; the tangential kick it adds is the visible part, and if playtesting says it still reads as nothing, raise the cap lift rather than adding an effect.
